unit.title: Testing Python code
unit.description: pytest, assert, test functions and files, fixtures, parametrize, testing exceptions, mocks, test-driven development, coverage, virtual environments

cards.definition: A unit test checks one function alone, in milliseconds. An integration test checks several parts together (code plus database, or plus a real API): slower, fewer, but closer to reality.
cards.example: Unit: add_vat(100) returns 120. Integration: the signup endpoint stores the lead in a test database.

cards.definition: A function decorated with @pytest.fixture that prepares data or resources for tests; a test receives it by naming it as a parameter.
@pytest.mark.parametrize runs the same test with several inputs and expected outputs, one line per case.
Checks that a piece of code raises the expected exception: with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse_price("abc").
cards.example: Testing that an empty email is refused.

cards.definition: A fake object that replaces a slow or external dependency (an API, the clock, an email service) during a test, so tests are fast, free and repeatable.
cards.example: Replacing requests.get with a mock that returns a fixed JSON.

cards.definition: Writing a failing test first, then the minimal code that makes it pass, then cleaning up: red, green, refactor. Very effective with AI coding agents, which can run the tests themselves.
cards.example: Write test_discount_caps_at_50_percent, see it fail, implement, see it pass.

cards.definition: The share of code lines (or branches) executed by the tests, measured with pytest-cov. Useful to find untested areas; a high number does not prove the tests check the right things.
cards.example: pytest --cov=app shows that the refund function was never run by any test.

exercises.prompt: Which file and function will pytest run automatically?
choices: test_prices.py with def test_vat():
prices_check.py with def check_vat():
tests.txt with a line test vat
main.py with def run_tests():
exercises.explain: pytest collects files named test_*.py (or *_test.py) and functions starting with test_.

exercises.prompt: This test fails. What does pytest show?
choices: The assert line with both values: 119.99 == 120
Only the word FAILED, with no details
Nothing: failing tests are skipped
A crash of the Python interpreter
exercises.explain: pytest rewrites asserts to show the compared values, which makes most failures obvious at once.

exercises.prompt: How does a test receive the data prepared by a fixture named leads?
choices: By having a parameter called leads
By importing leads from pytest
By calling fixture("leads") inside it
By reading a global variable
exercises.explain: pytest injects fixtures by parameter name. Each test gets a fresh copy by default.

exercises.prompt: How many tests does this produce?
exercises.explain: One test per tuple in the list. Each case is reported separately.

exercises.prompt: How do you check that parse_price("abc") raises a ValueError?
choices: with pytest.raises(ValueError): parse_price("abc")
assert parse_price("abc") == ValueError
try parse_price("abc") and print the error
assert ValueError in parse_price("abc")
exercises.explain: pytest.raises fails the test if no exception, or the wrong one, is raised.

exercises.prompt: Your function calls a paid weather API. How do you test it?
choices: Replace the API call with a mock returning fixed data
Call the real API in every test run
Skip testing that function entirely
Test it only once in production
exercises.explain: Mocks make tests fast, free and repeatable. One separate integration test can still hit the real API now and then.

exercises.prompt: In TDD, you write the test first, watch it fail, then write the code that makes it pass.
exercises.explain: True. Red, green, refactor. A test that never failed may be testing nothing.

exercises.prompt: Why give each project its own virtual environment?
choices: To isolate package versions between projects
To make Python run twice as fast
To hide the code from other users
Because pytest only runs inside one
exercises.explain: Project A can use pandas 2 while project B still needs pandas 1, without conflicts.

exercises.prompt: Coverage is 100 percent. What does it prove?
choices: Every line ran, not that the results are right
The code has no bugs left in it at all
Every possible input was tested too
The tests always run in under a second
exercises.explain: Coverage shows what was executed. Assertions on the right behaviour are what catch bugs.

exercises.prompt: This test always passes, even when the function is broken. Which line is the problem?
exercises.explain: A comparison without assert computes True or False and throws it away. Write assert price == 80.
